newsitem.title: USA: Southern Natl to lay off 1,000 after merger.
newsitem.headline: Southern Natl to lay off 1,000 after merger.

text.p: Southern National Corp said on Monday that approximately 1,000 workers would be let go once it completed its merger with United Carolina Bancshare Corp in the 1997 second quarter.
The two North Carolina banks revealed merger plans earlier Monday, whereby Southern National would absorb United Carolina Bancshares (UCB) for $985 million, or $40.01 per share.
"About 1,000 positions will be eliminated through attrition or early retirement," Southern National Chairman John Allison said, noting some 9,500 workers would remain.

Allison told reporters during a conference call that the details of the retirement package had not been worked out, but said a one-time charge of between $40 million and $50 million would be made in 1997 to cover merger-related expenses.
He said the expenses would cover costs for the severance program as well as closing branches in the estimated 80 locales where Southern National and UCB overlap.
Southern National operates 425 banking offices in 219 cities throughout the Carolinas and Virginia while UCB operates 153 offices in 89 communities in the Carolinas.
Although the deal was expected to have annual cost savings of $65 million, it would immediately dilute the Winston-Salem, N.C.-based bank's earnings by $0.08 per share, Allison said.
By June of 1997 "there will be eight cents per share projected dilution, excluding the one-time charge," he said.
But by the third quarter of 1998, the merger was expected to pay off, becoming accretive to earnings by $0.05 per share, Allison added.
As for profitability, he set targets for return on equity of 20 percent, up from 18.71 percent in the third quarter, and likewise return on assets of 1.65 percent, up from 1.48.
Once the merger is complete, the bank expects its efficiency ratio, or what it costs to earn $1, will be about 50 percent, down from 53.3 percent in the third quarter.
Allison, who took the helm of Southern National after the 1994 acquisition of Branch Banking & Trust Financial Corp, described the UCB deal as walking the "razor's edge."

He said the more recent round of acquisitions made by the bank -- a high-risk finance company and insurance firm -- asserts the bank's goal to remain independent but also increases its attractiveness to any possible suitors.
"It is truly a walk on the razors edge," Allison said.
UCB Chairman Rhone Sasser, who joined Allison on the conference call, told reporters the sale was in the best interest of shareholders, citing advances in technology.
Like other midsized banks, UCB cannot match the product and service offerings of larger banks, such as a vast automated teller machine network or banking by computer.

"With the cost of technology, additional rsources, and the level of competition we were facing, all of us know the sum is greater than the parts. This is one of those situations," Sasser said. He declined to comment on whether UCB talked with other suitors.
